body.html: Acid-base balance is the set of mechanisms keeping blood H⁺ constant: plasma pH 7.37 to 7.43, despite a daily acid load mainly from protein metabolism. Regulation relies on buffers, then the lungs, then the kidneys. Any serious imbalance can be incompatible with life.

An acid donates protons, a base accepts them; pH = -log [H⁺]. Plasma [H⁺] is about 40 nmol/L (pH 7.4); intracellular about 100 nmol/L (pH 7). Protons come from diet (protein; plants are mostly alkaline) and metabolism: volatile acid (CO₂), eliminated by the lungs through carbonic anhydrase; fixed acids, organic (lactic acid, ketone bodies) or mineral (phosphoric, sulphuric), highly dissociated and eliminated by the kidneys as free H⁺ (with bicarbonate reabsorption) or bound to NH₄⁺ and NaH₂PO₄.

A buffer is an acid/base pair; Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log [A⁻]/[AH]; buffering is strongest when pKa is close to pH and concentration is high. Bicarbonate/carbonic acid: the main extracellular buffer, immediate first line, efficient thanks to its high concentration, its pKa and ventilatory control, but consumed over time: pH = 6.1 + log [HCO₃⁻] / (0.03 × PCO₂). Proteinate: low capacity. Phosphate (NaH₂PO₄/Na₂HPO₄): low capacity, important in urine. Haemoglobin/haemoglobinate: high-capacity red-cell buffer; HbO₂ releases O₂ and binds H⁺ in tissues; in the lung H⁺ joins HCO₃⁻ to give CO₂. Bone proteins, phosphates and carbamates help in acidosis.

Lungs: rapid; medullary and peripheral chemoreceptors are very sensitive to pH. Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂; metabolic alkalosis → hypoventilation raises it. Limited capacity.

Kidneys: slower but more powerful and lasting, against both acidosis and alkalosis. (1) Reabsorb filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule; above 28 mmol/L bicarbonate is excreted. (2) Excrete H⁺ and regenerate bicarbonate: a little free H⁺ (urine pH down to about 4.4, exchanged for Na⁺ in the distal tubule; hence acidosis ↔ hyperkalaemia through H⁺/K⁺ exchange); most H⁺ bound: one third as titratable acidity (H₂PO₄⁻) and two thirds as ammonium (NH₄⁺), stimulated by acidosis and hyperkalaemia. Each mmol of H⁺ excreted generates one mmol of new HCO₃⁻.

Blood gases: arterial puncture (radial, femoral; capillary in newborns), single-use heparinised syringe, strictly anaerobic and sealed, analysed within an hour, on ice, gently mixed; note temperature, respiratory status, atmospheric pressure. Bicarbonate: heparin tube, no EDTA, citrate or oxalate. Values: pH 7.37 to 7.43 (corrected for temperature: pH - 0.014 × (T - 37)); PaCO₂ 37 to 43 mmHg; PaO₂ 75 to 100 mmHg; HCO₃⁻ 22 to 26 mmol/L; SaO₂ 95 to 99%. Anion gap = (Na⁺ + K⁺) - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 12 ± 2 mEq/L; lactate 1 to 2 mmol/L; ketone bodies.

Disorders: metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.38, HCO₃⁻ < 22, compensatory PaCO₂ fall); respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.38, PaCO₂ > 42 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ rises); metabolic alkalosis (pH > 7.42, HCO₃⁻ > 26, PaCO₂ rises); respiratory alkalosis (pH > 7.42, PaCO₂ < 36 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ falls). Mixed acidosis: PaCO₂ up and HCO₃⁻ down; mixed alkalosis: the reverse.

The adrenal medulla is a sympathetic ganglion that became a gland. It makes catecholamines, mostly adrenaline, for fight or flight. Two tumours matter: pheochromocytoma in adults and neuroblastoma in children.

Phenylalanine → tyrosine → dopa (tyrosine hydroxylase, the feedback step) → dopamine → noradrenaline → adrenaline (PNMT). Secretion is driven by splanchnic nerves (low BP, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, pain, stress, exercise) and helped by ACTH and cortisol.

ReceptorEffects
Beta-1Heart rate and force up; lipolysis
Beta-2Bronchodilation; renin; glycogenolysis; smooth muscle relaxation
Alpha-1Vasoconstriction; sphincter contraction
Alpha-2Inhibits noradrenaline release

Higher output and BP, mydriasis, less gut motility, glands inhibited except sweat, lipolysis, insulin inhibition, hyperkalaemia, thermogenesis.
COMT (70 percent) makes metanephrines; MAO (20 percent) degrades noradrenaline in nerve endings. Urine: VMA 80 percent, metanephrines 10 to 15 percent, free catecholamines 5 percent.

Calcium and phosphorus build the skeleton, but they are also vital: calcium for neuromuscular excitability, enzymes, membrane transport, hormone action and clotting; phosphorus for activating molecules (sugar-phosphates), ATP, enzyme regulation, phospholipids and nucleic acids, and acid-base buffering. Their metabolisms are linked and regulated by three organs (bone, intestine, kidney) and three hormones (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D).

Needs: 800 to 1,000 mg/day in adults, 1.2 g/day in growth, pregnancy, lactation and menopause (milk, cheese, mineral waters). Distribution: about 1 kg (25 mol), 99% in bone. In serum, half is diffusible (45% ionised, 5% complexed) and half is protein-bound, mostly (80%) to albumin. Absorption: mainly duodenum (acid helps); active, calcitriol-dependent, saturable transport when intake is low; passive transport takes over above about 600 mg/day. Elimination: stool, and urine (only the ultrafilterable half is filtered; 95% is reabsorbed; all when calcaemia is low, only half when it is high).

Needs: 1 g/day (1.2 to 1.4 g/day in pregnancy and lactation). About 600 g (0.8% of body mass): 85% bone, 14% intracellular, 1% extracellular. Organic (ATP, phospholipids) and inorganic forms; 90% of inorganic phosphate is ultrafilterable (HPO4²⁻ 80%, H2PO4⁻ 20%). Absorbed in the jejunum and ileum, in proportion to intake (active calcitriol-dependent plus passive). Renal: 90% reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, in competition with glucose.

PTH: 84 amino acids from the parathyroids; cleaved in liver and kidney, the N-terminal fragment carries the activity. It increases bone resorption, intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption of calcium, with the opposite effect on phosphate: hypercalcaemic, hypophosphataemic. Calcitonin: from thyroid parafollicular cells; fixes calcium and phosphate on bone, no direct gut action, lowers their renal reabsorption: hypocalcaemic, hypophosphataemic. Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, the most active vitamin D metabolite): resorbs old bone and mineralises new bone, increases gut absorption and renal reabsorption of both: hypercalcaemic, hyperphosphataemic. Other hormones affect bone without regulating the balance: oestrogens (more absorption and mineralisation), thyroid hormones (more turnover), cortisol (less mineralisation and absorption).

Calcaemia: morning, fasting; tourniquet neither too tight nor too long (venous stasis concentrates proteins and falsely raises calcium); no EDTA, citrate or oxalate (they chelate calcium). Reference 85 to 105 mg/L (2.25 to 2.60 mmol/L). Calciuria on 24-hour urine in a plastic or decalcified glass bottle. Because half of calcium is protein-bound, correct it: corrected Ca = measured Ca (mmol/L) + (40 - albumin g/L)/40, or measured Ca / [0.55 + (protein g/L)/160]. Phosphate (inorganic, fasting): adult 30 to 40 mg/L, child 40 to 60 mg/L. Hormones: PTH (useful in hypercalcaemia) and vitamin D.
Three questions, three markers: Is this an infarction? Troponin. Is this heart failure? BNP or NT-proBNP. What is the long-term coronary risk? Ultrasensitive CRP.

Old markers (myoglobin, CPK, CK-MB, AST, LDH) are not specific. Cardiac troponins T and I are; troponin C is shared by all muscle.

TimingValue
Rise (high-sensitivity)2 hours
Rise (conventional)4 hours
PeakAbout 14 hours
cTnI stays up75 to 140 hours
cTnT stays upOver 10 days

Also raised in myocarditis, toxicity, pericarditis. Assays are not standardised: use one lab.

BNP and NT-proBNP from cardiomyocytes are diuretic, natriuretic and vasodilator. They diagnose chronic heart failure, but rise with age and in women, fall with high BMI, and NT-proBNP is distorted in renal failure. Keep the same peptide and lab.
CRP: liver, IL-6; rises at 6 to 7 h, peaks at 48 to 72 h, normal by one week. A persistent low CRP signals cardiovascular risk.

Liver tests sort damage into three patterns: cytolysis (cells dying: AST, ALT), cholestasis (bile blocked: ALP, GGT, bilirubin) and insufficiency (the liver failing at its jobs: albumin, clotting, ammonium).

1.5 kg, 1500 mL/min (75 percent portal). Lobule is the unit. Functions: metabolism and urea cycle, protein synthesis (albumin, clotting factors), detoxification (bilirubin conjugation), and bile (1 L/day, micelles for fat).
ALT is liver-specific; AST also in heart and muscle (avoid haemolysis). Normal under 45 IU/L (men), 35 (women). Very high in acute hepatitis. LDH is non-specific (LDH5 liver).

Consequences: steatorrhoea, ADEK malabsorption, pale stools; pruritus (bile acids), jaundice, cholesterol up.

MarkerKey points
ALPLiver and bone; high in children and pregnancy; cholestasis, bone disease, cancers
GGTMost sensitive; isolated rise = chronic alcoholism; rises with ALP in cholestasis
Bilirubin3.4 to 17.1 µmol/L; jaundice in eyes above 30, skin above 50; protect from light

Insulin is the body's only glucose-lowering hormone. It is released when glucose enters the beta cell and sets off a ATP → K+ channel closure → Ca2+ entry chain, and it tells liver, muscle and fat to store fuel.
A chain 21, B chain 30 amino acids, three disulphide bridges; gene on chromosome 11. Preproinsulin → proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide.
Glucose → ATP up → K+ channels close → depolarisation → voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open → exocytosis. Insulin then activates its own gene to refill stores.

MetabolismActivatesInhibits
CarbohydrateGlycogenesis, glycolysis, pentose pathwayGluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, glucose release
LipidTriglyceride synthesis, fatty acid uptakeLipolysis
ProteinAmino acid uptake, anabolismCatabolism
GenesGlucokinase, pyruvate kinase, fatty acid synthaseGluconeogenic genes

Diagnosis: fasting glucose, HbA1c, urine glucose and ketones, OGTT for prediabetes. Monitoring: glucose monthly, HbA1c every 2 to 3 months, fructosamine (15 days) if haemoglobinopathy, lipids, microalbuminuria, creatinine.

Iron is essential for erythropoiesis. Iron deficiency is the commonest nutritional deficiency, especially in women and infants. The iron balance ('bilan martial') is interpreted with the clinical context (bleeding, inflammation, liver disease), age and sex.

A healthy adult has about 4 g. Haem iron (Fe²⁺): 60% (2.4 g) in haemoglobin, 5% in myoglobin, traces in respiratory enzymes. Non-haem iron (Fe³⁺): stores (ferritin and haemosiderin, 1.4 g, 35%) and plasma iron on transferrin (0.05 g). Macrophages destroy old red cells; the iron is stored or carried by transferrin back to the marrow; small amounts are lost in urine, desquamation, hair and nails, and episodically in menstruation and pregnancy.

Needs: 1 mg/day (men), 2 mg/day (women), 3 mg/day in the first two trimesters of pregnancy and 10 mg/day in the third; higher in infancy and adolescence. Sources: meat, fish, pulses; offal is richest. Absorption: duodenum and upper jejunum, about 10% of intake (so intake should be 10 mg in men, 20 mg in women), helped by vitamin C and acid; animal (haem) iron is absorbed better than plant iron; absorption falls with overload and rises with increased erythropoiesis (bleeding, haemolysis).

Transferrin, made mainly by hepatocytes, binds two ferric iron atoms and is about one-third saturated; its synthesis rises when stores fall and falls in overload. Transferrin receptors are richest on erythroblasts; a truncated soluble receptor (sTfR) reflects marrow activity.

Stores are about one third of body iron, in liver, spleen and marrow. Ferritin (apoferritin + ferric iron) is readily mobilised; macrophage ferritin is used first, hepatocyte ferritin only afterwards. Plasma ferritin (about 150 µg/L; 80% glycosylated from macrophages) reflects stores well. Haemosiderin releases iron slowly and stains with Perls' Prussian blue. Hepcidin, from the liver, is induced by excess iron and blocks iron exit from enterocytes and macrophages; low iron lowers hepcidin.

Serum iron alone is useless: HAS (2011) recommends measuring iron with transferrin. Sample fasting, no iron therapy for a week, no haemolysis. Serum iron: men 10 to 30 µmol/L, women 8 to 28. Transferrin: 2.4 to 3.8 g/L. TIBC = transferrin (g/L) × 25 (60 to 95 µmol/L). Transferrin saturation = iron / (25 × transferrin) × 100: men 20 to 40%, women 15 to 35%. Functional iron: Hb, MCV, MCHC, and sTfR (rises in deficiency). Ferritin (no daily cycle): men 30 to 300, women 20 to 200, children 15 to 100 µg/L.

Deficiency: losses (chronic digestive bleeding in the elderly, genital bleeding in women, pregnancy, lactation, prematurity, blood donation, haemodialysis) or poor intake (infants, elderly, pregnancy; malabsorption: IBD, chronic diarrhoea, gastrectomy, bowel resection). It develops in three phases: latent deficiency, proven deficiency, anaemia. WHO anaemia: Hb under 120 g/L (women) or 130 g/L (men), microcytic (MCV under 80 fL), hypochromic. Ferritin is the first-line test: under 30 µg/L with anaemia is enough; transferrin saturation (under 16%) falls only late and is a poor diagnostic test.

Primary haemochromatosis: autosomal recessive, usually HFE mutation, which lowers hepcidin; non-transferrin-bound iron loads the liver, heart and pancreas. Signs: melanoderma, hepatomegaly to cirrhosis, diabetes, pituitary hypogonadism, arrhythmias and heart failure, joint disease. Biology: high iron, low transferrin, very high saturation; ferritin rises late. Screening threshold: saturation over 45%, confirmed with ferritin over 200 (women) or 300 µg/L (men) and HFE genotyping. Secondary overload: haemolytic anaemias (ineffective erythropoiesis), repeated transfusions, haemodialysis supplementation, liver disease, atransferrinaemia. In inflammation, sTfR helps find a deficiency component.

Lipoprotein disorders are frequent and damage the arterial wall, so they are major cardiovascular risk factors. The lipid profile, now called Exploration of a Lipid Anomaly (ELA), is requested as a systematic check, for clinical signs (obesity, sedentary life, hypertension) and for treatment follow-up.

Lipids are insoluble, so they travel on albumin or inside lipoproteins: an apolar core of triglycerides and cholesterol esters, surrounded by phospholipids, free cholesterol and apoproteins. Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids) come from food or from sugars and alcohol via acetyl-CoA; they are the energy reserve. Cholesterol is one third dietary, two thirds hepatic; it builds membranes, steroid hormones and bile acids and is eliminated in bile (enterohepatic cycle). Phospholipids build membranes.

Apoproteins have a structural role (keep the complex soluble for transport) and a metabolic role (bind receptors, activate enzymes: apo AI activates LCAT). Five classes: A (AI, AII, AIV), B (B100, B48), C (CI, CII, CIII), D, E (E2, E3, E4).

Four classes: chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL, HDL. Chylomicrons are richest in triglycerides (86 to 94%), then VLDL (55 to 65%); LDL is rich in cholesterol esters (apo B100); HDL is rich in phospholipids and protein (apo A and C). The fattier a particle, the bigger and the less dense it is: chylomicrons float (density below 0.94) and are largest; HDL is the densest and smallest.

Endogenous: the liver makes triglycerides from glucose and free fatty acids and cholesterol from acetyl-CoA (about 800 mg/day). Exogenous: over 95% of dietary lipid is triglyceride; digested into monoglycerides and fatty acids, solubilised by bile acids, reassembled by enterocytes into chylomicrons that pass via lymph into blood.

Lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium hydrolyses the triglycerides of chylomicrons and VLDL into glycerol and fatty acids (energy or storage). Chylomicrons become remnants cleared by hepatic B/E receptors; VLDL become IDL, then LDL through hepatic triglyceride lipase. LDL binds receptors in liver and peripheral tissues; lysosomes free the cholesterol; excess returns to blood. HDL picks up excess free cholesterol, esterifies it via LCAT (anti-atherogenic), and delivers it to the liver or steroidogenic tissues.

Sampling: fast of at least 12 hours, rest 15 minutes, away from acute illness (viral infection, hepatitis, surgery; wait 3 to 4 months after an infarction), dry or heparin tube, no haemolysis. Serum appearance must be reported: clear (normal, but does not exclude hypercholesterolaemia), lactescent or creamy layer (chylomicrons), cloudy/opalescent (VLDL or IDL), cloudy with creamy supernatant (VLDL + chylomicrons).

Reference values: TG 0.5 to 1.5 g/L; total cholesterol 1.50 to 2 g/L; HDL 0.35 to 0.65 g/L; total/HDL ratio under 4.9 (men) and 4.2 (women). Friedewald: LDL = TC - HDL - TG/5 (g/L) or TG/2.2 (mmol/L), valid only if TG under 3.5 g/L (4 mmol/L); otherwise measure LDL directly or use Planella's formula.

LDL targets: under 4 mmol/L without risk factors, under 2.6 mmol/L with risk factors (men over 50 or women over 60, family history of early coronary disease, smoking, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, HDL under 1 mmol/L, microalbuminuria). Apo AI and B: the most accurate atherogenic risk measure; apo B 0.6 to 1.40 g/L, apo AI above 1.10 g/L; risk rises with the apo B/apo AI ratio.

Raised cholesterol and/or triglycerides, or high LDL with low HDL, contributing to atherosclerosis. Hyperlipoproteinaemias (about 4% of adults over 30) are primary (genetic) or secondary (disease or drugs). Hypocholesterolaemia (total cholesterol under 1.30 g/L) is hereditary or secondary (hyperthyroidism, severe liver disease). The Fredrickson classification types the disorders; type I is hyperchylomicronaemia.

Most wrong lab results are not wrong analyses: 68 percent of errors happen before the sample reaches the analyser. The preanalytical phase covers the prescription, the patient, the equipment, the sampling and the transport.

Give the time (cortisol, thyroid hormones, adrenaline vary daily), sex, age (ALP higher in children) and pregnancy (ALP up; proteins, iron, ferritin down by haemodilution). For an infusion, sample the opposite arm and state the infusion.

FactorRule
PostureRest 15 min in the same position
Exercise12 hours of rest (CK can quadruple)
FastingAt least 8 h, sample 7 to 9 a.m. (lipids +21 percent otherwise)
StressRaises prolactin, adrenaline, cortisol

Equipment carries a CE or FDA mark and meets EN/MN 14820. Tourniquet: 7 to 10 cm above, not tight, off within 1 minute (up to 10 percent error otherwise). Tubes: respect the order, never transfer blood, respect the fill (citrate 1:4), mix 5 to 10 times. Label immediately and check identity.

Upright; analyse within 2 hours (glucose falls; potassium and transaminases rise); store at 4 to 8°C; protect bilirubin from light. Haemolysis from tourniquet, syringe turbulence, agitation or delay falsely raises potassium and intracellular enzymes.

Routine renal exploration rests on three tests: creatinine, proteinuria and microalbuminuria, supported by the ionogram, calcium-phosphate and uric acid. Specialised tests (clearance, concentration and dilution) study glomerular and tubular function.

PotassiumOver 6.5 mmol/L life-threatening
Osmolality[(Na + K) x 2] + urea + glucose = 290
Calcium/phosphateCKD: Ca down, P and PTH up

Clearance = U x V / P. Creatinine clearance: men 130 ± 20, women 110 ± 20 mL/min per 1.73 m². Errors from incomplete collection; MDRD avoids them.

Clearance (mL/min)CKD
50 to 70Moderate
20 to 50Significant
5 to 20Severe
Under 5Dialysis or transplant
Concentration: overnight water fast, urine over 800 mOsm/kg. Dilution: 20 mL/kg water load, urine near 100 mOsm/kg, 80 percent excreted in 5 h.

Serum protein electrophoresis (PEP) separates serum proteins into five fractions in an electric field: albumin, alpha-1, alpha-2, beta and gamma globulins. The liver makes all serum proteins except gamma globulins, which come from lymphoid tissue. PEP gives a diagnostic orientation (not a confirmation), helps assess severity and follows treatment.

Proteins are amphoteric. In an alkaline buffer (pH 8.2 to 8.6) all serum proteins are negatively charged (anions), so they all migrate toward the anode (+). Speed depends on particle size, ionic strength and the porosity of the support. Albumin migrates fastest and furthest.

Use serum (dry tube or clot activator), never plasma on anticoagulant: plasma contains fibrinogen, which would appear as an extra band. Avoid haemolysis: haemoglobin would also appear as an extra band. If delayed, blood can be kept at 4 °C for up to a week.

Gel electrophoresis (agarose; blotting paper was the 1937 original): semi-automated; 0.1 mL of serum; several patients per gel; about 20 min of migration; amido black staining; a densitometer turns band intensity (optical density) into five peaks; about 90 min in total. Capillary zone electrophoresis: fully automated, faster, one patient at a time with same-day results. Results: the proteinogram (bands), the electrophoretic profile (peaks), and values in % and g/L; the A/G ratio is normally 1.2 to 1.8.

Albumin: transport, acid-base buffer, oncotic pressure. Alpha-1 and alpha-2: inflammatory proteins. Gamma: antibodies. Physiological: albumin falls in pregnancy and old age; alpha globulins rise in pregnancy; beta rises in pregnancy and at 40 to 70 years; gamma is low in infants and the elderly.

Pitfalls: a dye bubble (artefact peak), a large CRP (over about 100 to 150 mg/L, a peak in the gamma zone that should disappear with the inflammation), haemoglobin (splits alpha-2), fibrinogen (extra peak in the gamma zone).

Albumin: bisalbuminaemia (hereditary and harmless, or acquired, e.g. beta-lactams in renal failure); hypoalbuminaemia from low intake, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, severe inflammation. Alpha-1 ↓ alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; ↑ acute inflammation. Alpha-2 ↓ intravascular haemolysis (low haptoglobin); ↑ inflammation and nephrotic syndrome (alpha-2 macroglobulin). Beta ↓ C3 consumption in infection; beta-gamma block in alcoholic cirrhosis (polyclonal IgA). Gamma ↓ in infants and immune deficiency (primary or chemo/steroids); ↑ polyclonal (dome, infection) or monoclonal (narrow spike: myeloma, lymphoma, benign in the elderly).

PEP cannot type the monoclonal immunoglobulin: request immunofixation (six lanes with anti-IgG, IgA, IgM, kappa and lambda) to distinguish Kahler (myeloma) from Waldenström disease, which are treated differently. When to order PEP: high serum protein, unexplained high ESR, recurrent bacterial infections (hypogammaglobulinaemia), bone pain or hypercalcaemia (myeloma), suspected inflammation or cirrhosis.

Every steroid hormone is made from cholesterol through pregnenolone. Which one a tissue makes depends on its enzymes. The classic exam case is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, where a blocked enzyme shunts precursors into androgens.

SiteHormones
Adrenal glomerular zoneAldosterone
Adrenal fascicular zoneCortisol (some androgens)
Adrenal reticular zoneDHEA and androgens
OvaryOestradiol (follicles), progesterone (corpus luteum)
Testis (Leydig cells)Testosterone, 95 percent of total
PlacentaOestrogens (oestriol), progesterone

CarbonsHormones
C18Oestrogens: E1 (menopause), E2 (active women), E3 (pregnancy)
C19Androgens: DHEA, androstenedione, testosterone, DHT (most potent)
C21Progesterone, cortisol, aldosterone

Mitochondria: cholesterol → pregnenolone by 20-22 desmolase, the key enzyme, stimulated by ACTH, LH and FSH. Microsomes: progesterone and 17-OH derivatives, then:

  • Cortisol: 21- then 11-beta-hydroxylase; 20 mg/day; inactivated to cortisone.
  • Aldosterone: glomerular zone only, via deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone.
  • Androgens: DHEA (adrenal), testosterone (testes).
  • Oestrogens: by aromatase from androgens; fat takes over after menopause.

21-hydroxylase deficiency (CAH): 17-OH progesterone and androgens rise, cortisol and aldosterone fall, ACTH rises; ambiguous genitalia in girls, salt loss, early puberty.

Cortisol: stress, catabolism, anti-inflammatory, fetal lung surfactant. Aldosterone: Na+ in, K+ out at the distal tubule. Oestrogens: bone, sex traits, uterine excitability. Progesterone: implantation, uterine quiet. Androgens: anabolism, spermatogenesis.

CRH → ACTH → adrenal; GnRH → FSH (oestrogens) and LH (progesterone) → gonads.

The thyroid is a vital gland: life is not possible without thyroid hormones. Its job is to make T4 and T3 from iodine (from food) and tyrosine, inside a protein called thyroglobulin, stored in the colloid of the follicle.

Follow one chain: iodide in → oxidised by TPO → put on tyrosines (MIT, DIT) → coupled into T3 and T4 → released by lysosomes → carried by TBG → T4 turned into active T3 in the tissues → controlled by TRH and TSH. Most exam questions test one link of this chain, the free forms, or how a disease breaks it.

The thyroid is butterfly-shaped, in front of the trachea just below the larynx. Its functional unit is the follicle: a ball with a wall of a single layer of cubic epithelial cells (follicular cells, thyrocytes) around a central cavity of colloid.

  • Apical pole faces the colloid; basal pole faces the blood vessels.
  • Rich in granular ER, Golgi and apical vesicles: very active protein-synthesising cells that exchange molecules between blood and colloid.

StepWhat happens
1. Iodide capture and oxidationIodine comes from food. Follicular cells capture iodide (I⁻) by active transport (30 times the blood level). Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidises it to active organic iodine (I2) at the apex.
2. ThyronineTwo tyrosines (from the blood) condense into thyronine (two aromatic rings joined by an ether bridge).
3. ThyroglobulinMade in ribosomes, through ER and Golgi; vesicles discharge it into the colloid.
4. IodinationTPO binds iodine to tyrosines of thyroglobulin: MIT (one iodine), DIT (two).
5. CouplingTPO: DIT + DIT = T4 (thyroxine, 4 iodines); DIT + MIT = T3 (3 iodines). Reverse T3 is made and secreted but inactive. Hormones are still on thyroglobulin.
6. ReleaseThyroglobulin re-enters the cell by endocytosis; lysosomal enzymes separate the hormones. Only T3, T4 and reverse T3 are secreted. Deiodinase frees iodine from MIT and DIT for recycling.
7. SecretionT4 is the main hormone secreted (90%); part of T4 becomes T3 in the thyrocyte. Only T3 and T4 act. Only a very small free fraction circulates, and the free hormone is the active one: measuring FT4 and FT3 matters most in diagnosis.

CarrierKey point
TBG (thyroxine-binding globulin)The most important; made by the liver; binds T4 with very high affinity
TBPA (thyroxine-binding prealbumin)Binds mainly T3, less affinity for T4
AlbuminNon-specific carrier

Bound hormones are inactive. Each receptor binds only its own hormone (T3's receptor fits T3, T4's fits T4).

Most T3 is made in peripheral tissues: abundant T4 is converted to active T3 by deiodinase. T3 is 10 times more active than T4 and binds receptors in the cytoplasm (biological effects) and the nucleus (gene transcription for enzymes).

Regulation: a fall in T4 makes the hypothalamus release TRH, which makes the pituitary release TSH; TSH binds thyrocyte receptors and stimulates T4 secretion. A rise in T4 gives negative feedback on the hypothalamus-pituitary axis.

TSH: anterior pituitary glycoprotein, two subunits: an alpha chain common to TSH, LH, FSH and hCG, and a specific beta chain (modern assays target the beta chain to avoid false positives). TSH activates every step: iodine uptake and activation, TPO and thyroglobulin synthesis, secretion.

Catabolism:

  1. Conjugation with sulphuric or glucuronic acid in the liver; inactive products leave in the bile and stool.
  2. Deamination, decarboxylation, oxidation in liver and kidney → TRIAC and TETRAC (15% eliminated in stool).
  3. Deiodination in the kidney: iodine goes back to the thyroid if needed, otherwise into the urine. This is 80% of T4 degradation.

Thyroid hormones act on almost every organ, but above all on basal metabolism.

Tissue level:

  • Reproduction: a thyroid check-up is part of every couple's fertility work-up.
  • Nervous system: formation of neural structures and more connections (alertness, irritability).
  • Bone: they promote GH secretion and act in synergy with it. GH drives chondrogenesis and cartilage growth; thyroid hormones drive maturation and ossification of cartilage.
  • More adrenergic receptors in the vessels: higher pulse and systolic pressure.

Cellular level: heat production with more O2 use; faster metabolism: glycolysis and glycogenolysis ↑, lipolysis ↑, proteolysis giving a negative nitrogen balance.

HyperthyroidismHypothyroidism
Weight loss with appetite kept; heat intolerance, sweating; irritability, insomnia; hand tremor; tachycardia; proptosis; goitre or nodule; muscle weaknessWeight gain; slowed thinking, memory problems, depression; feeling cold; hair loss, dry pale skin; puffy eyes; slow heart rate; constipation; cramps; fatigue; goitre possible

Thyroid disease has two separate faces: morphological (goitre, nodule, cancer) and endocrine (hyper or hypo). A goitre can come with both: in peripheral hypothyroidism (e.g. iodine deficiency) constant TSH swells the gland with colloid; in central hyperthyroidism (TSH-secreting adenoma) TSH drives the gland too.

Causes of hyperthyroidism (excess FT4 and/or FT3; more women than men):

  1. Graves' disease: the most common; autoimmune, anti-TSH receptor antibodies that stimulate the receptor.
  2. Toxic adenoma (nodular goitre with warm nodules).
  3. Toxic multiheteronodular goitre (hot and cold nodules).
  4. Pregnancy: mutated TSH receptor that also binds hCG; disappears when hCG falls.
  5. Iatrogenic: iodine-containing amiodarone (check the thyroid before prescribing, then every 6 months; contraindicated if dysthyroid) and iodinated contrast (test far from the injection).
  6. Central: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Also thyroid cancer and testicular tumour (pseudo-TSH).

Causes of hypothyroidism:

  • Goitrous: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune; anti-thyroglobulin, anti-microsomal and anti-peroxidase antibodies; common in women); iodine deficiency (endemic goitre).
  • Others: TSH-receptor mutation (insensitive to TSH); after surgery or radiotherapy; congenital (agenesis or ectopia: cretinism and dwarfism); central (pituitary or hypothalamic).

• FT4: measures the active free fraction directly; makes the positive diagnosis of hyper- or hypothyroidism.
  • Ultrasensitive TSH (TSHus): detects very small changes; locates the problem as central or peripheral.
  • Etiology: e.g. anti-thyroglobulin antibodies for Hashimoto's.

Reading the pair (tutorial cases): high FT4 with low TSH = peripheral hyperthyroidism; low FT4 with high TSH = peripheral hypothyroidism; low FT4 with low or normal TSH = central hypothyroidism (a TRH test then separates pituitary from hypothalamic).

Replacement therapy: half-life T3 1 day, T4 1 week. T4 is preferred: once daily, better compliance, and it is converted to T3 in the tissues.

Electrolytes dissociate into ions in water; every fluid stays electrically neutral, and water moves between compartments mainly because electrolytes move. The plasma ionogram (with or without a urine ionogram) is a very common routine and emergency test for ionic and hydration disorders; the kidney is central to the balance.

Water is about 60% of body weight (42 L at 70 kg): less in women (50%), more in infants (75%), less in the elderly; 75% in muscle, 22% in bone, 10% in fat. A rapid weight change suggests water gain or loss. Intake: the lecture lists drinks 2.2 L, food 0.7 L and metabolic water 0.3 L per day, for a stated total of 2.5 L/day; output 2.5 L/day: urine 1.5, insensible losses (skin, lungs) 0.9, stool 0.1.

Intracellular: 40 to 50% of body weight, two thirds of water, 28 L. Extracellular (internal environment): 20% of body weight: interstitial 15% (12 L, a protein-poor plasma ultrafiltrate) and plasma 5% (3 L).

For a monovalent ion mEq = mmol (sodium 142 mmol/L = 142 mEq/L); for a divalent ion mEq = mmol × 2 (calcium 2.50 mmol/L = 5 mEq/L). Proteins are negative at physiological pH. Plasma: sodium is the main cation (potassium low); chloride the main anion, then bicarbonate and proteins. Intracellular: potassium is the main cation, phosphates the main anions, then proteins; little sodium and chloride. Interstitial fluid: like plasma without proteins, so anions ×1.05 and cations ×0.95 (Donnan equilibrium).

Cell membrane: electrolytes cross by diffusion or active transport (the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps sodium out); water follows osmosis, from hypotonic to hypertonic. Capillary: freely permeable to water and ions, not to proteins; Starling's law: at the arterial end hydrostatic pressure exceeds oncotic pressure and water leaves with O2 and nutrients; at the venous end oncotic pressure wins and water returns with CO2 and waste.

Extra-renal: water shifts and the thirst centre. Renal: ADH (hypothalamus, released by the pituitary) reabsorbs water alone in collecting ducts; RAAS: low blood pressure releases renin, the angiotensin pathway leads to aldosterone from the adrenal cortex, which retains sodium and water; ANF from the atria is diuretic, natriuretic and vasodilating.

Pre-analytical: avoid haemolysis and delays (release intracellular potassium); no sodium heparin (false sodium) or EDTA (false potassium); hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperproteinaemia cause false hyponatraemia; samples keep a week at 4 °C; 24-h urine without antiseptic.

Sodium (main extracellular cation, 90% extracellular, sets extracellular osmolality): 135 to 145 mmol/L. Hyponatraemia: sodium loss (renal, digestive), excess water, or reduced water excretion (ADH excess). Hypernatraemia: excess sodium (hypertonic saline), too little water, or water loss (renal: diuretics, hyperglycaemia; insensible: fever, hyperventilation, sweating; intestinal: diarrhoea). Potassium (main intracellular cation, excitability): 3.5 to 5.5 mmol/L. Hypokalaemia: constipation, cramps, hypotonia, cardiac signs; from vomiting, diarrhoea, hyperaldosteronism, tubulopathy, poor intake. Hyperkalaemia: life-threatening above 6.5 mmol/L (conduction disorders); from IV overload, renal failure, cell lysis (burns). Chloride (main extracellular anion): 95 to 108 mmol/L; varies with sodium and opposite to bicarbonate; high with NaCl or KCl infusion, tubulopathies, dehydration; low with vomiting or diuretics.

Osmolality (particles per kg of water) is well reflected by sodium: calculated = (Na + K) × 2 + urea + glucose = 280 to 300 mOsm/kg, or measured by osmometer; osmolarity (per litre) 280 to 295 mOsm/L. Extracellular dehydration: isotonic loss of water and sodium (vomiting, diarrhoea, heat stroke, renal failure). Intracellular dehydration: pure water deficit (respiratory losses on intubation, inability to drink after head injury, diabetes insipidus). Global: cystic fibrosis, infant gastroenteritis, diabetes. Extracellular hyperhydration (oedema): sodium excess in renal failure, heart failure, cirrhosis. Intracellular hyperhydration: falling osmolarity from sodium loss or dilution.
